newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jordan's king warns of violence, PLO holds out hope.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's king warns of violence, PLO holds out hope.

text.p: Jordan's King Hussein warned on Wednesday there was a "very strong chance of violence" if Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushed ahead with plans for a Jewish settlement on the outskirts of Arab East Jerusalem.
Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat voiced hope a meeting of U.S., European and Arab envoys on Saturday would rescue Middle East peace from a deepening crisis over Israeli policies.

Israeli-Palestinian relations -- which warmed briefly after the Jewish state pulled its troops from most of the West Bank town of Hebron in January under a peace deal -- have plunged to turmoil over recent Israeli decisions, notably approval last month of 6,500 new houses for Jews in the holy city's Arab half.
In New York the United Nations General Assembly began a debate expected to end in overwhelming support for a demand that Israel abandon its plans to build on the site.
Netanyahu's settlement policy in East Jerusalem, which both Israelis and Palestinians claim as their capital, has also taken a sudden toll in the Jewish state's ties with Jordan.

"I think if it happens there is a very strong chance of violence," King Hussein told the Cable News Network (CNN), referring to the planned settlement at a pine-covered hilltop called Jabal Abu Ghneim by Palestinians and Har Homa by Israel.

"There is an air of crisis," King Hussein said. The Middle East was "sliding towards the abyss of extremism", and Arafat had been reduced to a state of "complete despair" by the lack of progress in his talks with Israel, he said.
Arafat, asked why he had called the weekend forum of envoys for in the Gaza Strip, said, "To protect the peace process."

The United States, Israel's closest ally, tightened the noose of international pressure around the Jewish state on Wednesday by saying it would send Edward Abington, the consul general in Jerusalem, to the Gaza meeting.

"We regard this as a briefing on Arafat's concerns about the peace process," said Ambassador Martin Indyk in defence of U.S. participation despite the objections raised by Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy when they met on Wednesday.
Wrapping up a visit to Moscow, Netanyahu was combative when asked about mounting world criticism of his policies.
He told a Moscow news conference he was "fed up" with charges Israel was violating peace deals with the Palestinians.
But there were signs world pressure might be taking effect.

Israel Radio quoted Deputy Housing Minister Meir Porush as telling a parliamentary panel on Wednesday that "legal and administrative" matters would keep bulldozers from breaking ground for the new settlement on Sunday, as originally planned.
Hawks called this evidence of caving in to Arab pressure.

King Hussein, departing from customarily measured responses to Israeli policies, warned Netanyahu against high-handed treatment of Palestinians, saying: "You cannot humiliate a people and continue to do it without having any reaction."
The king has been Netanyahu's closest Arab ally. But he sent a sharply-worded rebuke to the Israeli Prime Minister this week saying he could no longer consider him a serious peace partner.

Palestinians accuse Netanyahu of trying to circumvent them as his peace partners and of violating Israeli-PLO peace accords by planning to build the settlement, which they say compromises talks due to decide the fate of East Jerusalem by 1999.

Palestinian wrath was further stoked by Israel's decisions to hand over less than a third of the West Bank land the PLO expected in a withdrawal planned for this month, and by warnings Israel would close four Palestinian offices in East Jerusalem.
"Does Israel really think that the world approves and would stay silent? Israel will realise sooner or later that it is wrong and the world is right," PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat said.
Arafat refused to take two telephone calls from Netanyahu on Monday, Israeli media said. A PLO official said Arafat refused more than twice since Friday to receive Netanyahu's aides.
"He doesn't want to talk. We won't force him," Netanyahu said. "I think there's an attempt to create a crisis."
